questions.prompt: The author's discussion in the third sentence of the passage is intended primarily to

choices.text: substantiate the claim that the demand for electricity will climb 50 percent by the year 2010
undermine the claim that efficient energy use is an effective means of addressing environmental problems caused by increased energy demand
specify the time frame within which it will be necessary to develop renewable energy technology
offer evidence for the claim that fossil fuels are a problematic source of electricity
foreshadow a claim concerning the need for localized involvement in environmentally sound technological development

questions.prompt: Which one of the following, if true, would most call into question the author's assertion in the last sentence of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
When we're doing Strengthen / Weaken in RC, we often see question stems asking us to impact a *claim / assertion* rather than an *argument*.

That often means we have less up front work to do!

We don't need to think about conclusion vs. evidence; we just need to look at the individual assertion.

The author is asserting that the wind turbine project in India has a good change of remaining competitive and profitable for the long run, given that the Danish agency that helped India build these turbines also helped trained Indians to plan / operate / maintain / construct these turbines.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Let's look for an answer that gives us a way to be pessimistic about the long-term viability of this Indian wind turbine project.

The correct answer should fit logically within this sentence:
*The Indian wind turbine project is **not** going to remain competitive and profitable in the long run, because ... [answer choice].*

choices.text: The profitability of the India project was due primarily to temporary subsidies from the Indian government.
choices.explanation:
This seems to work.

*The Indian wind turbine project is **not** going to remain competitive and profitable in the long run, because ...* it was only profitable in the short term because of **temporary** subsidies from the Indian government.

Once those subsidies stop, the project will probably not be profitable anymore.

choices.text: The Danish energy agency invested more funds in the India project than the U.S. agency invested in the Brazil project.
choices.explanation: A larger investment does not by itself explain away current profitability or establish that it depends on support that will disappear. A makes that temporary dependency explicit; B does not. We cannot infer a definite strengthening or weakening effect from the funding comparison alone.

choices.text: Indian firms are not required to limit user fees charged to consumers.
choices.explanation:
Does it make any sense to say,

*The Indian wind turbine project is **not** going to remain competitive and profitable in the long run, because ...* Indian firms are not required to limit user fees charged to consumers?

It would make more sense to say that "it's unlikely to be profitable in the long run because they **have** to limit the fees they charge to customers".

The fees charged to customers are the revenue side of profitability. If there's a limit to what they can charge, then maybe the revenue won't be able to outpace expenses in order to remain profitable.

But since this is saying that Indian firms *aren't* limited in terms of what user fees they can charge, that means they have leeway to charge high fees and thus have a profitable business.

choices.text: Environmental pollutants are produced in the manufacture of some equipment used in wind turbines.
choices.explanation:
This sounds vaguely negative in relation to the wind turbine project, but the negative thing doesn't directly relate to profitability or competitiveness. And it's a super weak idea because it's just saying "*some* equipment used in wind turbines involves environmental pollutants in the manufacturing process".

That's probably true of almost every manufacturing process in the world. Most of them produce *some* environmental pollutant, so it's not persuasive to say that "because the manufacturing process for some turbine parts involves producing some environmental pollutants, this wind turbine industry won't be profitable in the long run".

Its competition (i.e. the fossil fuel extraction and refining industry) certainly produces its share of environmental pollutants, so this doesn't show a comparative disadvantage of wind turbines.

choices.text: New technology is poised to decrease sharply the level of pollutants produced by fossil-fuel plants.
choices.explanation: Cleaner fossil-fuel technology might affect competition, but the answer does not establish how customers, prices or the Indian project's revenue would respond. A directly identifies temporary subsidies as the main source of current profitability. E requires additional assumptions to challenge the project's long-term profitability.

passages.title: Victorian Philanthropists
passages.text:
Although philanthropy—the volunteering of private resources for humanitarian purposes—reached its apex in England in the late nineteenth century, modern commentators have articulated two major criticisms of the philanthropy that was a mainstay of England’s middle-class Victorian society. The earlier criticism is that such philanthropy was even by the later nineteenth century obsolete, since industrialism had already created social problems that were beyond the scope of small, private voluntary efforts. Indeed, these problems required substantial legislative action by the state. Unemployment, for example, was not the result of a failure of diligence on the part of workers or a failure of compassion on the part of employers, nor could it be solved by well-wishing philanthropists.

The more recent charge holds that Victorian philanthropy was by its very nature a self-serving exercise carried out by philanthropists at the expense of those whom they were ostensibly serving. In this view, philanthropy was a means of flaunting one’s power and position in a society that placed great emphasis on status, or even a means of cultivating social connections that could lead to economic rewards. Further, if philanthropy is seen as serving the interests of individual philanthropists, so it may be seen as serving the interests of their class. According to this “social control” thesis, philanthropists, in professing to help the poor, were encouraging in them such values as prudence, thrift, and temperance, values perhaps worthy in themselves but also designed to create more productive members of the labor force. Philanthropy, in short, was a means of controlling the labor force and ensuring the continued dominance of the management class.

Modern critics of Victorian philanthropy often use the words “amateurish” or “inadequate” to describe Victorian philanthropy, as though Victorian charity can only be understood as an antecedent to the era of state-sponsored, professionally administered charity. This assumption is typical of the “Whig fallacy”: the tendency to read the past as an inferior prelude to an enlightened present. If most Victorians resisted state control and expended their resources on private, voluntary philanthropies, it could only be, the argument goes, because of their commitment to a vested interest, or because the administrative apparatus of the state was incapable of coping with the economic and social needs of the time.

This version of history patronizes the Victorians, who were in fact well aware of their vulnerability to charges of condescension and complacency, but were equally well aware of the potential dangers of state-managed charity. They were perhaps condescending to the poor, but—to use an un-Victorian metaphor—they put their money where their mouths were, and gave of their careers and lives as well.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Victorian philanthropy in England—its criticisms and reassessment

**Framework**

Present Debate (with a touch of Challenge Position, since the author is pushing back at the end)

**Main Point**

Modern critics have major complaints about Victorian philanthropy, often viewing it as outdated or self-serving, but these criticisms may be too simplistic and overlook the intentions and awareness of the Victorian philanthropists themselves. ("This version of history patronizes the Victorians, who were in fact well aware of their vulnerability to charges of condescension and complacency, but were equally well aware of the potential dangers of state-managed charity." - last paragraph)

**P1: Introduction and First Criticism**

We’re introduced to Victorian philanthropy and the first big critique: it was basically outdated because huge industrial-era social problems demanded government intervention rather than individual charity efforts.

**P2: Second Criticism—Self-Serving Motives**

The second major critique is that Victorian philanthropy was ultimately a form of self-promotion and class control. Under this view, charity let philanthropists show off their status while molding the poor to be better workers, benefitting the management class.

**P3: Critics and the "Whig Fallacy"**

Modern critics often label Victorian philanthropy as naive or amateurish, mainly judging it as inadequate compared to modern, professional, state-run charity. This, the author says, falls into the “Whig fallacy”—viewing the past as just a less enlightened forerunner to the present.

**P4: Author Pushes Back and Nuances the Picture**

The author argues that this historical perspective is unfair. The Victorians were aware of the risks of both private and state-led charity—they may have been condescending, but their philanthropy involved real commitment, and their motivations weren’t as simple as critics make out.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best summarizes the main idea of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic of the passage is *Victorian philanthropy*.

Why is the author writing about it? What's his purpose? What framework did we use?

He's discussing these two major criticisms of Victorian philanthropy. Is it to present a debate, or to weigh in with his own opinion?

The 3rd paragraph is where we begin to hear the author's voice, but on our 1st read it's pretty tricky to pick up on the attitudinal markers.

He says, "Modern critics often say X or Y to describe Z, as though Z could only be understood as ____ . "

That construction indicates disagreement. We might hear, "Paul often says either his older boy or his younger boy have the best shot at being professional athletes, as though only his male children have a good chance at being professional athletes".

That person would be *Challenging* Paul's *Position*, suggesting that maybe he's wrong and maybe one of his daughters actually has the best shot at being a pro athlete.

The 1st sentence of the 3rd paragraph presents that negative innuendo. If we're thinking, "Is that the author being saucy? Is this a clapback? Is this a *Challenge Position* passage?!", then our suspicions are strengthened when the next sentence says, "This assumption [the critics are making] is typical of the Whig **fallacy**."

The final sentence of the 3rd has a similar sarcasm as the first sentence of the 3rd.

*(1st) Critics say ___ , **as though X could only be understood** as ___ .*
*(3rd) If most Z's were doing ___ , **it could only be, the argument goes**, because of ___ .*

Both of these constructions are sarcastic eye-rolls. The author is *not* buying their logic, and he's making fun of the critics for getting boxed into a narrow and incorrect way of thinking.

The 4th paragraph, though, makes it most clear that this is a *Challenge Position* passage, because it begins "This version of history patronizes the Victorians".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Since we have a *Challenge Position* passage about Victorian philanthropists, the main point should either sound like "[what the critics said] about Victorian philanthropists is wrong", or sound like "here is what we *should* be saying about Victorian philanthropists".

So let's look for something like,
"It's wrong to call Victorian philanthropy amateurish or inadequate, just because it wasn't powerful enough to solve major social problems and because it may have allowed rich people the moral satisfaction of helping while still keeping the poor dependent on them."

Or something like, "We should give the Victorian philanthropists some credit. Yeah, they didn't solve massive social problems, but they tried, even while being self-aware that people would call them out on being condescending with their help".

choices.text: While the motives of individual practitioners have been questioned by modern commentators, Victorian philanthropy successfully dealt with the social ills of nineteenth-century England.
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is somewhat tempting, because it's an affirmational positive about the Victorian philanthropists:

*Victorian philanthropy successfully dealt with the social ills of the 19th century England.*

While the author has a positive view, he is more saying, "Hey, at least they **tried** to fix social ills", not "they **succeeded** in fixing social ills".

The author agrees in the 1st paragraph with the notion that "industrialism had already created social ills that were *beyond* the scope of small, private voluntary efforts".

He says, "**Indeed**, these problems required substantial legislative action by the state".

choices.text: Philanthropy, inadequate to deal with the massive social and economic problems of the twentieth century, has slowly been replaced by state-sponsored charity.
choices.explanation:
The main clause of this answer is:
*Philanthropy has slowly been replaced by state-sponsored charity.*

Since the main clause doesn't even mention our central topic (Victorian philanthropy) this is not worth reading on a first pass.

Also this main clause has nothing to do with the author's *Challenge Position* purpose. The author's main point wasn't "philanthropy has been replaced by state-sponsored charity".

His main point was, "Stop hatin' on my Victorian philanthropists, critics. At least they tried to do good."

choices.text: The practice of reading the past as a prelude to an enlightened present has fostered revisionist views of many institutions, among them Victorian philanthropy.
choices.explanation:
The main clause of this answer is:
*The practice of reading the past as a prelude to an enlightened present has fostered revisionist views of many institutions.*

Since the main clause doesn't even mention our central topic (Victorian philanthropy) this is not worth reading on a first pass. Yes, the answer does mention Victorian philanthropy, but only as an aside. It was one example of many.

Meanwhile, the passage is *only* about Victorian philanthropy!

choices.text: Although modern commentators have perceived Victorian philanthropy as either inadequate or self-serving, the theoretical bias behind these criticisms leads to an incorrect interpretation of history.
choices.explanation:
The main clause of this answer is:
*The theoretical bias behind these criticisms [of Victorian philanthropy] leads to an incorrect interpretation of history.*

This main clause by far has the strongest sound of a *Challenge Position* purpose. "An incorrect interpretation" of history sounds like what an author would say if he's rejecting the way critics interpret these Victorian philanthropists.

Let's see if we can sign off on all the details.

Do modern commentators perceive Victorian philanthropy as either inadequate or self-serving?

Yes! There are two major criticisms:
1. (P1) This type of philanthropy was already obsolete, since industrialism had already created problems beyond the scope of small, private voluntary efforts (thus, inadequate)

2. (P2) The more recent charge holds that Victorian philanthropy was by its very nature self-serving.

The author rejects these in the 3rd paragraph by calling out the *Whig fallacy* assumption that undergirds these two criticisms. That *Whig fallacy* is the "theoretical bias" the answer is referring to.

choices.text: Victorian philanthropists, aware of public resentment of their self-congratulatory attitude, used devious methods to camouflage their self-serving motives.
choices.explanation:
The main clause of this answer is:
*Victorian philanthropists used devious methods to camouflage their self-serving motives.*

That sounds really negative! That doesn't sound like our author. Our author is defending the Victorian philanthropists / sticking up for them / *Challenging the Position of critics who belittle them.*

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of both modern criticisms made about Victorian philanthropy?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Is there any common ingredient to these two criticisms?

Criticism 1:
the problems are too big to be tackled by philanthropy. they're caused by huge forces such as industrialization and can only be really be solved by big governmental action.

Criticism 2:
you rich people are just doing philanthropy to show off how noble and enlightened you are. meanwhile, you're teaching poor people values that will allow you to continue enjoy your elite position while they continue to be subjugated.

It doesn't seem like there's really much overlap there, other than a pessimism that the philanthropy wasn't actually doing great things, wasn't lifting people out of poverty and oppression.

We might have to try these answers on for size and see if we can support them with each criticism.

choices.text: Both criticisms attribute dishonorable motives to those privileged individuals who engaged in private philanthropy.
choices.explanation: Only criticism 2 impugns the philanthropists for having self-serving (dishonorable) motives. Criticism 1 is fine believing this was well-intentioned, genuine stuff. It's just saying, "you're deluding yourselves -- these problems are too big for you to solve."

choices.text: Both criticisms presuppose that the social rewards of charitable activity outweighed the economic benefits.
choices.explanation: The second criticism mentions both status and possible economic rewards, without ranking the social rewards above the economic benefits. The first criticism does not make that comparison either. The answer therefore adds a shared comparison that neither discussion establishes.

choices.text: Both criticisms underemphasize the complacency and condescension demonstrated by the Victorians.
choices.explanation: In the final paragraph, the author is saying that these criticisms overemphasize the condescension and complacency of the Victorians. Our author defends the philanthropists by saying, "Stop acting like they were complacent and condescending. They were self-aware about how their efforts could be viewed that way, and commendably they went ahead an tried anyway."

choices.text: Both criticisms suggest that government involvement was necessary to cure social ills.
choices.explanation:
This is well supported by criticism 1, which was essentially saying exactly this: the attempt by wealthy individuals to try to tackle these huge problems is never gonna amount to a significant fix. These problems "require substantial legislative action by the state".

Where do we get support for this from the 2nd type of critics?

The 3rd paragraph refers to "modern critics of Victorian philanthropy". Seemingly this encompasses both the 1st and 2nd type of criticism, since both of those are identified in the 1st paragraph as belonging to "modern commentators". And the 2nd type of criticism is also identified as the "more recent".

So if the 3rd paragraph is talking about both of these types of critics together (or even skewing towards the 2nd type). we can use this text as ammunition as well.

That first sentence is saying that both types of modern critics *often use the words "amateurish" or "inadequate" to describe Victorian philanthropy, as though Victorian charity can only be understood as an antecedent to the era of state-sponsored, professionally administered charity.*

That implies that both types of critics saw Victorian philanthropy as *inadequate*, not up to the task of solving the big problems it targeted. An inferior attempt before the superior era of state-sponsored government involvement stepped in.

choices.text: Both criticisms take for granted the futility of efforts by private individuals to enhance their social status by means of philanthropy.
choices.explanation:
The 1st criticism isn't talking about whether or not the philanthropic attempts were an effort to enhance social status, so we have no support there.

And the 2nd criticism wasn't saying that these efforts were futile; if anything, it makes it seem like philanthropists WERE able to cultivate social connections that could lead to economic rewards.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best describes the attitude of the author of the passage toward the "Whig" interpretation of Victorian philanthropy?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The author's final paragraph shows that she doesn't much appreciate the modern criticisms of Victorian philanthropy. She thinks that the Victorian philanthropists were pretty self-aware that they might be seen as condescending or inadequate, but they still put forth money and effort to do the right thing.

The 3rd paragraph begins with some eye-rolling sarcasm.

She is saying that critics describe the Victorian philanthropy as "amateurish" or "inadequate" because they see it as obviously inferior to the era of state-sponsored, professionally administered charity.

It's like comparing the efforts of some neighborhood friends who decide to make sandwiches for the homeless to the efforts of some official non-profit organization that has more robust infrastructure and resources.

Sure, the latter is more effective than the former, but should we really make fun of the former? Should we mock the people who made sandwiches for the homeless and call their efforts "amateurish" or "inadequate"?

The author says that the attitude the critics have towards Victorian philanthropy is a familiar one, dubbed "the Whig fallacy", in which people evaluate the past as inferior and consider the present the superior / enlightened time period.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something negative, because the author doesn't appreciate this Whig fallacy interpretation of Victorian philanthropy.

choices.text: strong disagreement
choices.explanation:
The author's 3rd and 4th paragraphs are both criticizing this Whig interpretation, so we know she disagrees with it.

In the 3rd paragraphs, the author is mocking them by sarcastically playing along with their thinking -- "Victorian philanthropy **can only** be understood as an antecedent to 'superior' state-sponsored charity", and "If most Victorians expended their resources on private, voluntary philanthropies, it **could only** be, the argument goes, because of their vested interest."

Not to mention, it's called the Whig **fallacy** for a reason -- the author thinks it's fallacious / wrong to think that way.

choices.text: mild skepticism
choices.explanation:
The author spends two paragraphs to punch back at this interpretation, so it's not going far enough to say that she's just mildly skeptical.

*Mild skepticism* would sound more like, "**But perhaps** this version of history is unfairly patronizing to the Victorians".

Instead, we have "this version of history is patronizing to the Victorians. This is a fallacy of thinking that earlier stuff is therefore inferior."

choices.text: cynical amusement
choices.explanation:
Cynical amusement is what some people get when they go on Twitter and doomscroll. The world is ending, and it's kind of fun to watch.

The author wrote this passage specifically to disagree with these modern critics, so saying her attitude is *cynical amusement* makes it seem like she wants to sit back and enjoy their mistakes and wrongness.

But she isn't amused. She's actually getting in the ring and challenging the Whig interpretation to a fight.

choices.text: bland indifference
choices.explanation: The author identifies the critics' assumption as a fallacy and says their interpretation patronizes the Victorians. That is an evaluative objection, not indifference. Whether a neutral attitude could be correct in a different question has no bearing on the evidence here.

choices.text: unqualified support
choices.explanation:
*Unqualified Support* means that you support something wholeheartedly, with no qualms whatsoever.

Our author does not like the Whig interpretation, so this is more like the opposite of what we want.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best describes the primary purpose of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
For *Primary Purpose* questions, we mainly think about our Framework.

Since the 3rd and 4th paragraphs revealed that this was a *Challenge Position* passage, we want an answer to sound like that:

- push back against a point of view
- find fault with an interpretation
- defend a phenomenon against criticism
- etc.

choices.text: providing an extended definition of a key term
choices.explanation:
Providing a long definition sounds more *informative* than *opinionated*.

Furthermore, there was not any long definition of a key term. Presumably, the key term would be 'philanthropy', but it's not like the main reason the author wrote this passage was to provide a lengthy definition of 'philanthropy'.

choices.text: defending the work of an influential group of theorists
choices.explanation:
This starts off how we want it, because the author *is* defending the Victorian philanthropists against the unwarranted, in the author's view, criticisms.

But are the Victorian philanthropists "an influential group of theorists"?

Heck no. They were just rich people who spent some of their money trying to help the poor.

choices.text: narrating the chronological development of a widespread practice
choices.explanation:
Narrating a long chronological story sounds more like an informative, reporting-style passage than it does the opinionated rebuttal this passage was.

Presumably, the widespread practice this answer refers to would match up with 'philanthropy', but the author didn't tell a long chronological story about how philanthropy developed.

This passage all takes place in one time / place / era, Victorian England.

choices.text: examining modern evaluations of a historical phenomenon
choices.explanation:
This is the closest we get to *Challenging the Position* of the critics.

The "modern critics" are offering their modern evaluation of a historical phenomenon, Victorian philanthropy.

The author is challenging this evaluation.

Does the verb "examine" mean "to challenge"? No, it's not clear when you examine something whether you have a positive, negative, or neutral evaluation of it.

But the author *does* examine these modern criticisms/evaluations. She delineates what they are / she explains the theoretical bias that's behind them / and then she critiques them.

Sometimes *Primary Purpose* questions use a verb that indicates an opinion took place, but doesn't indicate whether the opinion was positive or negative.

If we wrote a scathing review of a restaurant on Yelp that was multiple paragraphs long, and LSAT asked what the primary purpose of our writing was, a correct answer could say,

(A) to list out all the bad things about the meal we had

But a sneakier correct answer could say,

(A) to evaluate the quality of the dining experience at a restaurant

Yes, that answer doesn't reveal the fact that our evaluation is very negative, but it's not saying anything untrue. We *did* write that review to evaluate / judge / examine the quality of the dining experience.

choices.text: analyzing a specific dilemma faced by workers of the past
choices.explanation:
The central topic of the passage is Victorian philanthropy and what modern critics say about it.

Philanthropists aren't considered "workers". Even though we can say we do charitable work, the context of this passage was that these philanthropists were rich people willing to help out the poor. We wouldn't call those rich people "workers" for involvement in helping out the poor.

Even if we accepted "workers of the past" as an abstract name for "Victorian philanthropists", the passage's central focus wasn't to analyze a specific problem Victorian philanthropists faced.

It was to say to these modern critics, "stop hatin' on my Victorian philanthropists. At least they tried to do some good."

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that a social control theorist would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements concerning the motives of Victorian philanthropists?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The "social control" theorists are talked about in the second half of the 2nd paragraph. Overall, the 2nd paragraph is saying that Victorian philanthropy was mainly about rich people trying to feel better about themselves by helping the less fortunate.

It was sort of "showing off how generous you were", centuries before social media would let us do that with even less effort!

But the question stem is asking about what social control theorists would say about ****the motives**** of the philanthropists. Where do the social control theorists specifically talk about motives?

*Philanthropists were encouraging in the poor such values as prudence, thrift, and temperance, values perhaps worthy in themselves but also* *****designed to***** *create more productive members of the labor force. Philanthropy* *****was a means of***** *controlling the labor force and ensuring continued dominance of the management class.*

The closest match for philanthropists' motives are revealed by what their efforts were designed to do, what ends their philanthropy was a means of accomplishing.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something that essentially means the Victorian philanthropists were motivated by wanting to control the labor force, make laborers more productive, while continuing to dominate them.

choices.text: Victorian philanthropists were driven more by the desire for high social status than by the hope of economic gain.
choices.explanation: We're supposed to be matching this answer to the last two sentences of the 2nd paragraph, and high social status is not mentioned in either of those sentences.

choices.text: Victorian philanthropists encouraged such values as thrift and temperance in order to instill in the working class the same acquisitiveness that characterized the management class.
choices.explanation:
The 2nd to last sentence of the 2nd paragraph says that they encouraged such values to create *more productive* members of the labor force, not to instill *the qualities that they*, the management class, possessed.

I'll be honest; I've never seen acquisitiveness (and I'm a vocab nerd). I just looked it up and it means "desire to ****acquire**** material possessions", so that's definitely a mismatch. It's also counterintuitive.

The philanthropists wouldn't be encouraging being thrifty in order to instill a lust for material possessions.

Not knowing the meaning of that obscure word, we'd be wise to keep this on the first pass. It didn't seem like it would be right purely from the sense of its gist that "the philanthropists were motivated to instill the same qualities they had". That sounds too benevolent. The social control theorists are suggesting something more sinister and depressing -- "the philanthropists were trying to perpetuate their elite dominance and control labor, while making them more productive".

choices.text: Though basically well-intentioned, Victorian philanthropists faced problems that were far beyond the scope of private charitable organizations.
choices.explanation:
We're supposed to be matching this answer to the last two sentences of the 2nd paragraph, and "well-intentioned" seems like the opposite of "ensuring their continued dominance".

"Problems that were far beyond the scope of private organizations" is also not mentioned there.

choices.text: By raising the living standards of the poor, Victorian philanthropists also sought to improve the intellectual status of the poor.
choices.explanation: We're supposed to be matching this answer to the last two sentences of the 2nd paragraph, and "improving intellectual status of the poor" is not mentioned in either of those sentences, just "making them work harder / controlling them / dominating them".

choices.text: Victorian philanthropists see philanthropy as a means to an end rather than as an end in itself.
choices.explanation:
This is supported by the last sentence of the 2nd paragraph:

Philanthropy, in short, ****was a means**** of controlling the labor force and ensuring continued dominance. It wasn't about helping the poor, as an end in itself. It was about helping the poor enough that they could be more productive workers while accepting their subjugated role in a society controlled by the philanthropists.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following best describes the organization of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The shortcut we often have available on Organization questions is to primarily focus on the *last* ingredient of the passage.

Here, we know that the last two paragraphs were where the author mounted her *Challenge* to the position of the modern commentators.

So let's head to the answers and read the last ingredient first, to see if we can make it work for the final paragraph. If so, we'll see whether every other ingredient in the answer can match up.

choices.text: Two related positions are discussed, then both are subjected to the same criticism.
choices.explanation:
"Subjected to criticism" sounds like an acceptable way to describe the last paragraph (as well as the second to last). Does the rest of the answer make sense?

Sure, the very first sentence of the passage announces that modern commentators have articulated ****two major criticisms (i.e. positions)****. The rest of paragraph 1 discusses the first position (victorian philanthropy was inadequate). Paragraph 2 discusses the second position (victorian philanthropy was self-serving).

And then paragraphs 3 and 4 consist of the author critiquing these modern commentators, saying "Y'all think that the past is always inferior to the present, and you're failing to recognize that Victorian philanthropists may have been sensitive to critiques of inadequacy or self-glorification, but they nonetheless at least *tried* to help out those in need".

choices.text: Two opposing theories are outlined, then a synthesis between the two is proposed.
choices.explanation: "A synthesis is proposed" is not a good match for the ending of this passage, which is where the author is criticizing the modern views, not synthesizing them.

choices.text: A position is stated, and two differing evaluations of it are given.
choices.explanation: There are two positions presented (the two major criticisms of modern commentaors) and then one evaluation given (the author's). This is reversing that and saying that one position was stated, and then two different evaluations were given.

choices.text: Three examples of the same logical inconsistency are given.
choices.explanation: This answer makes it seem like the final paragraph(s) was a 3rd example of a logical inconsistency. That doesn't make any sense at all. We just want to hear that the ending was where the author pushed back against the views of these modern commentators.

choices.text: A theory is outlined, and two supporting examples are given.
choices.explanation: This answer makes it seem like the final paragraph(s) was a 2rd example of something. That doesn't match up. We just want to hear that the ending was where the author pushed back against the views of these modern commentators.

passages.title: Rita Dove
passages.text:
For decades, there has been a deep rift between poetry and fiction in the United States, especially in academic settings; graduate writing programs in universities, for example, train students as poets or as writers of fiction, but almost never as both. Both poets and writers of fiction have tended to support this separation in large part because the current conventional wisdom holds that poetry should be elliptical and lyrical, reflecting inner states and processes of thought or feeling, whereas character and narrative events are the stock-in-trade of fiction.

Certainly it is true that poetry and fiction are distinct genres, but why have specialized education and literary territoriality resulted from this distinction? The answer lies perhaps in a widespread attitude in U.S. culture, which often casts a suspicious eye on the generalist. Those with knowledge and expertise in multiple areas risk charges of dilettantism, as if ability in one field is diluted or compromised by accomplishment in another.

Fortunately, there are signs that the bias against writers who cross generic boundaries is diminishing; several recent writers are known and respected for their work in both genres. One important example of this trend is Rita Dove, an African American writer highly acclaimed for both her poetry and her fiction. A few years ago, speaking at a conference entitled “Poets Who Write Fiction,” Dove expressed gentle incredulity about the habit of segregating the genres. She had grown up reading and loving both fiction and poetry, she said, unaware of any purported danger lurking in attempts to mix the two. She also studied for some time in Germany, where, she observes, “Poets write plays, novelists compose libretti, playwrights write novels— they would not understand our restrictiveness.”

It makes little sense, Dove believes, to persist in the restrictive approach to poetry and fiction prevalent in the U.S., because each genre shares in the nature of the other. Indeed, her poetry offers example after example of what can only be properly regarded as lyric narrative. Her use of language in these poems is undeniably lyrical—that is, it evokes emotion and inner states without requiring the reader to organize ideas or events in a particular linear structure. Yet this lyric expression simultaneously presents the elements of a plot in such a way that the reader is led repeatedly to take account of clusters of narrative details within the lyric flow. Thus while the language is lyrical, it often comes to constitute, cumulatively, a work of narrative fiction. Similarly, many passages in her fiction, though undeniably prose, achieve the status of lyric narrative through the use of poetic rhythms and elliptical expression. In short, Dove bridges the gap between poetry and fiction not only by writing in both genres, but also by fusing the two genres within individual works.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The institutional separation of poetry and fiction in U.S. literary culture, and the writer Rita Dove as evidence that the divide is breaking down.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy. The author flags a long-standing rift, criticizes the cultural attitudes behind it, and uses Rita Dove's career as the lead example of an encouraging shift.

**Main Point**

The U.S. tendency to wall off poetry from fiction may stem from a suspicion of generalists, but writers like Rita Dove — who not only work in both genres but fuse them within individual works — show the divide is unnecessary and that the bias against cross-genre writers is fortunately fading.

**P1: A long-standing rift**

For decades U.S. graduate writing programs have trained students as poets or as fiction writers — almost never both. Both camps have largely supported the split, on the assumption that poetry handles inner states while fiction handles character and narrative.

**P2: Where the rift comes from**

Poetry and fiction really are distinct genres, but the author proposes that the territorial separation may reflect a U.S. cultural suspicion of generalists — an attitude that treats expertise in multiple fields as dilettantism.

**P3: Signs the bias is fading; enter Rita Dove**

Some recent writers, notably Rita Dove (who works in both genres), are respected across the line. Dove finds the segregation puzzling and notes that German writers move freely among genres without the same restrictiveness.

**P4: Dove fuses the genres**

Dove's poetry uses lyrical language while still carrying narrative detail, producing "lyric narrative." Her prose, conversely, uses poetic rhythms. Dove bridges the gap by working in both genres and by fusing them within individual works.

summaries.anotherWay:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The author is talking about a wall in U.S. literature: poets do one thing, fiction writers do another, and they don't mix. Then they bring in Rita Dove as a writer who simply ignores the wall.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy. The author isn't fighting an opponent — they're flagging a problem and pointing to someone who shows the problem is unnecessary.

**Main Point**

Here's the simpler version: in the U.S., poets and fiction writers stay in their lanes, and writing programs reinforce that. The author thinks this comes from a broader American attitude that doesn't trust people who do more than one thing well. But the wall is starting to come down — and Rita Dove is the headline example, both because she works in both genres and because she fuses them inside individual works.

**P1: The rift**

Most of paragraph 1 sets the scene: poetry and fiction are taught and practiced as separate worlds. The reasoning has been that poetry is for inner experience and fiction is for plot and character.

**P2: Why the rift exists**

The author asks why a real distinction between two genres turned into territorial separation, and suggests that U.S. culture’s distrust of the generalist may explain it. If you do two things, people assume you're diluting both.

**P3: The bias is fading; meet Dove**

"Fortunately" is the giveaway: the author is glad the bias is shrinking. Several writers are now respected across the divide. Dove is the lead example — she grew up loving both genres and points out that German writers move freely between genres without the same suspicion.

**P4: Dove blends the two**

Dove doesn't just write poetry and fiction; she fuses them. Her poems carry narrative arcs even while staying lyrical. Her prose uses poetic rhythms. The author calls this "lyric narrative" and treats Dove's practice as the bridge between the two genres.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Rita Dove’s work has been widely acclaimed primarily because of the lyrical elements she has introduced into her fiction.
choices.explanation: The passage does not state why Rita Dove’s work has been widely acclaimed.

choices.text: Rita Dove’s lyric narratives present clusters of narrative detail in order to create a cumulative narrative without requiring the reader to interpret it in a linear manner.
choices.explanation: This describes part of how lyric narrative works in paragraph 4. The main point is broader: Dove's work exemplifies a trend away from the rigid separation of poetry and fiction. The answer leaves that trend and her fiction's poetic elements out.

choices.text: Working against a bias that has long been dominant in the U.S., recent writers like Rita Dove have shown that the lyrical use of language can effectively enhance narrative fiction.
choices.explanation: This answer fails to account for Rita Dove’s use of narrative in her poetry.

choices.text: Unlike many of her U.S. contemporaries, Rita Dove writes without relying on the traditional techniques associated with poetry and fiction.
choices.explanation: The passage suggests that Rita Dove uses traditional techniques such as evoking emotion and inner states (fourth paragraph).

choices.text: Rita Dove’s successful blending of poetry and fiction exemplifies the recent trend away from the rigid separation of the two genres that has long been prevalent in the U.S.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the third paragraph.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following is most analogous to the literary achievements that the author attributes to Dove?

choices.text: A chef combines nontraditional cooking methods and traditional ingredients from disparate world cuisines to devise new recipes.
choices.explanation: Rita Dove used traditional methods.

choices.text: A professor of film studies becomes a film director and succeeds, partly due to a wealth of theoretical knowledge of filmmaking.
choices.explanation: The relationship in this answer is causal, whereas the passage is primarily concerned with the blending of literary genres.

choices.text: An actor who is also a theatrical director teams up with a public health agency to use street theater to inform the public about health matters.
choices.explanation: Rita Dove blended genres within the field of literature, whereas this answer describes a combination of unrelated fields to solve a specific problem.

choices.text: A choreographer defies convention and choreographs dances that combine elements of both ballet and jazz dance.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the last paragraph.

choices.text: A rock musician records several songs from previous decades but introduces extended guitar solos into each one.
choices.explanation: Guitar solos are a common feature of rock music, so this answer does not refer to a blend of two distinct genres.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, in the U.S. there is a widely held view that

choices.text: poetry should not involve characters or narratives
choices.explanation: This is supported at the end of the first paragraph.

choices.text: unlike the writing of poetry, the writing of fiction is rarely an academically serious endeavor
choices.explanation: The passage indicates that both poetry and writing were taught in universities (first paragraph).

choices.text: graduate writing programs focus on poetry to the exclusion of fiction
choices.explanation: The passage indicates that both poetry and writing were taught in universities (first paragraph).

choices.text: fiction is most aesthetically effective when it incorporates lyrical elements
choices.explanation: The passage does not say when fiction is most aesthetically effective.

choices.text: European literary cultures are suspicious of generalists
choices.explanation: The only American view of European literary culture represented in the passage indicates an openness on the part of Europeans to generalists (third paragraph).

questions.prompt: The author's attitude toward the deep rift between poetry and fiction in the U.S. can be most accurately described as one of

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
This is an Author's Attitude question about the rift between poetry and fiction. Throughout the passage the author treats the split as a problem:

- P2 traces it to a cultural suspicion of generalists
- P3 calls it "fortunate" that the bias is fading
- P4 holds up Dove as an exemplar of crossing the divide.

So the attitude is is definitely negative.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for a negative answer and judge its nuances from there.

choices.text: perplexity as to what could have led to the development of such a rift
choices.explanation:
Since the author, in P2, suggests a possible answer to the question of what caused the rift, it's hard to say the author is totally at a loss for where this came from.

The author might be undecided about what caused the rift, but perplexed is more like baffled.

choices.text: astonishment that academics have overlooked the existence of the rift
choices.explanation:
*Astonished* is a very strong descriptor, so this would need some good text support.

But more importantly, the passage never claims academics have overlooked the rift; it kinda says the opposite.

P1 is saying graduate writing programs **institutionalize** the rift by training students as one or the other.

choices.text: ambivalence toward the effect the rift has had on U.S. literature
choices.explanation:
Ambivalence implies mixed feelings — partly positive, partly negative.

The author's view of the rift is uniformly negative: it comes from a problematic cultural attitude (P2), and the author is "fortunately" seeing it diminish (P3).

There's no positive commentary we can point to.

choices.text: pessimism regarding the possibility that the rift can be overcome
choices.explanation:
The author is the opposite of pessimistic. P3 begins with "Fortunately, there are signs that the bias against writers who cross generic boundaries is diminishing."

The whole final third of the passage celebrates Dove as evidence that the rift can be overcome.

choices.text: disapproval of attitudes and presuppositions underlying the rift
choices.explanation:
We know the author disapproves of the rift, because she says "Fortunately" the rift is diminishing (P3).

Does she disapprove of the attitudes and assumptions underlying it? Yes, that's basically the substance of P2.

The author traces the rift to specific underlying attitudes, a U.S. cultural suspicion of generalists and the assumption that ability in one field is "diluted or compromised" by accomplishment in another (P2).

For non-native speakers ----
When we use the expression "as if", we're implying that it's not the case.

*People who are tall are suspected of being good at basketball, as if tallness implied athleticism.*

This sentence is saying that some people assume that "if you're tall, you're athletic".

questions.prompt: In the passage the author conjectures that a cause of the deep rift between fiction and poetry in the United States may be that

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Where in the passage is the author ruminating about why there's a deep rift between poetry and fiction in the US?

The first line of the passage explicitly mentions this rift, and the rest of the first paragraph goes on to describe how this rift plays out (no one studies both / different expectations for each genre).

But it's not until the second paragraph that we dig into the causal backstory of the rift. The author asks, "*****Why***** *have specialized education and literary territoriality resulted from this distinction? The answer lies* *****perhaps***** *in ...* "

This speculative answer (perhaps) is a ****conjecture****. So we know we've locked in on the right moment of the passage. Now we just have to comprehend it.

The author says that there's a widespread attitude in US culture that *casts a suspicious eye on the generalist.*

What is a generalist? Well, the opposite of general is specific. So the opposite of a specialist would be a generalist. A doctor who does heart transplant surgeries is probably a specialist -- she knows everything there is to know about heart transplants.

Meanwhile, a primary care physician (an internist) would be more of a generalist. They have basic knowledge of a lot of stuff, but refer you to specialists when they're in over their head.

So US cultures apparently trusts specialists, and has a suspicious eye toward generalists. If you have "knowledge and expertise in ****multiple**** areas", we worry that you're a jack of all trades, master of none.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Applying this to the rift between poetry and fiction, it sounds like the author is conjecturing that there's a deep rift because people don't believe that you could really be great at both. You should either be specializing in poetry or in fiction, because if you try to dabble in both, you'll be an unsophisticated dilettante (jack of all trades, master of none).

choices.text: poets and fiction writers each tend to see their craft as superior to the others’ craft
choices.explanation: The passage does not say whether poets or fiction writers see their craft as superior to the other.

choices.text: the methods used in training graduate students in poetry are different from those used in training graduate students in other literary fields
choices.explanation: The passage does not say what methods are used in training poets and other literary fields..

questions.prompt: If this passage had been excerpted from a longer text, which one of the following predictions about the near future of U.S. literature would be most likely to appear in that text?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
Do we ever hear anything about "the near future of U.S. literature"?

Yes, it's kind of the main point. The author gives us a Theme / Example setup at the beginning of P3.

TREND: the bias against writers who cross genre boundaries is diminishing

EXAMPLE: Rita Dove crosses genre boundaries (poetry + fiction) and is highly acclaimed.

Nothing else in the passage seems to be discussing a current / future trend.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for an answer that sounds like people are increasingly embracing the idea of writers who mix genres / defy boundaries.

choices.text: The number of writers who write both poetry and fiction will probably continue to grow.
choices.explanation:
This is our best match. We were hoping to see evidence that the bias *against* writers who mix genres (such as poetry + fiction) is diminishing.

This doesn't speak to how well-received these hybrid writers are, but there's some causal common sense logic that the more hostility there is towards a type of writing, the fewer writers who will be willing to do that style / endure that hostility.

As the friction against blending genres diminish, more writers will be unafraid to do so. So this answer best matches the available support window.

choices.text: Because of the increased interest in mixed genres, the small market for pure lyric poetry will likely shrink even further.
choices.explanation:
The passage doesn't discuss the market for "pure lyric poetry" or any other market share.

We know that mixed genres will be better received, but that doesn't mean that un-mixed genres (*pure* poetry) will do WORSE.

choices.text: Narrative poetry will probably come to be regarded as a sub-genre of fiction.
choices.explanation:
Reclassifying narrative poetry as a sub-genre of fiction is a big change in genre taxonomy, and the author is just saying that there's less bias against mixing genres.

This is going a big step further and saying that literary critics will decide to make a hybrid form a sub-genre of fiction.

Why wouldn't it be a sub-genre of poetry?

The passage hasn't given any reason to think that if a writer uses a blend of fiction and poetry, we'll ultimately come to categorize it as a subgenre of fiction.

choices.text: There will probably be a rise in specialization among writers in university writing programs.
choices.explanation: We're looking for "it'll become increasingly acceptable to mix genres", and this is saying it'll be increasingly common to specialize in one genre.

choices.text: Writers who continue to work exclusively in poetry or fiction will likely lose their audiences.
choices.explanation: This is similar to (B). We were told that mixed genre writing will be more accepted, but that doesn't mean that single-genre writing will be less accepted.

passages.title: The Capacity for Music
passages.text:
*The two passages discuss recent scientific research on music. They are adapted from two different papers presented at a scholarly conference.*

**Passage A**

Did music and human language originate separately or together? Both systems use intonation and rhythm to communicate emotions. Both can be produced vocally or with tools, and people can produce both music and language silently to themselves.

Brain imaging studies suggest that music and language are part of one large, vastly complicated, neurological system for processing sound. In fact, fewer differences than similarities exist between the neurological processing of the two. One could think of the two activities as different radio programs that can be broadcast over the same hardware. One noteworthy difference, though, is that, generally speaking, people are better at language than music. In music, anyone can listen easily enough, but most people do not perform well, and in many cultures composition is left to specialists. In language, by contrast, nearly everyone actively performs and composes.

Given their shared neurological basis, it appears that music and language evolved together as brain size increased over the course of hominid evolution. But the primacy of language over music that we can observe today suggests that language, not music, was the primary function natural selection operated on. Music, it would seem, had little adaptive value of its own, and most likely developed on the coattails of language.

**Passage B**

Darwin claimed that since “neither the enjoyment nor the capacity of producing musical notes are faculties of the least [practical] use to man they must be ranked amongst the most mysterious with which he is endowed.” I suggest that the enjoyment of and the capacity to produce musical notes are faculties of indispensable use to mothers and their infants and that it is in the emotional bonds created by the interaction of mother and child that we can discover the evolutionary origins of human music.

Even excluding lullabies, which parents sing to infants, human mothers and infants under six months of age engage in ritualized, sequential behaviors, involving vocal, facial, and bodily interactions. Using face-to-face mother-infant interactions filmed at 24 frames per second, researchers have shown that mothers and infants jointly construct mutually improvised interactions in which each partner tracks the actions of the other. Such episodes last from one-half second to three seconds and are composed of musical elements— variations in pitch, rhythm, timbre, volume, and tempo.

What evolutionary advantage would such behavior have? In the course of hominid evolution, brain size increased rapidly. Contemporaneously, the increase in bipedality caused the birth canal to narrow. This resulted in hominid infants being born ever-more prematurely, leaving them much more helpless at birth. This helplessness necessitated longer, better maternal care. Under such conditions, the emotional bonds created in the premusical mother-infant interactions we observe in *Homo sapiens* today—behavior whose neurological basis essentially constitutes the capacity to make and enjoy music—would have conferred considerable evolutionary advantage.

summaries.standard:
******Main Point (Passage A)******

Music, it would seem, had little adaptive value of its own, and most likely developed on the coattails of language (lines 25–27).

******Passage Map (Passage A)******

****P1**** - A question about music and language is posed.
****P2**** - Music and language are compared.
****P3**** - An answer to the question is offered—music developed on the coattails of language.

******Main Point (Passage B)******

I suggest that the enjoyment of and the capacity to produce musical notes are faculties of indispensable use to mothers and their infants and that it is in the emotional bonds created by the interaction of mother and child that we can discover the evolutionary origins of human music (lines 32–37).

******Passage Map (Passage B)******

****P1**** - A hypothesis is offered about the origins of music.
****P2**** - A phenomenon is described.
****P3**** - An explanation of that phenomenon is offered, which supports the hypothesis.

questions.prompt: Both passages were written primarily in order to answer which one of the following questions?

choices.text: What evolutionary advantage did larger brain size confer on early hominids?
choices.explanation: Brain size is part of the support in both passages, but not part of the question initially posed in passage A (first paragraph of passage A) or the mystery to be explained in passage B (first paragraph of passage B).

choices.text: Why do human mothers and infants engage in bonding behavior that is composed of musical elements?
choices.explanation: This is only addressed in passage B (last paragraph) and is not the main point of passage B.

choices.text: What are the evolutionary origins of the human ability to make music?
choices.explanation: Passage A asks whether music and language originated separately or together, then argues that music likely evolved alongside language. Passage B proposes an evolutionary origin in mother-infant bonding. Both therefore address the evolutionary origins of the ability to make music.

choices.text: Do the human abilities to make music and to use language depend on the same neurological systems?
choices.explanation: Passage A, paragraph 2 discusses a shared neurological system. That evidence supports its account of music's origins; the shared-system question is not the primary concern of both passages.

choices.text: Why are most people more adept at using language than they are at making music?
choices.explanation: Passage A, paragraph 2 contrasts performance in language and music. The passage uses that contrast in its evolutionary argument, but neither passage is primarily trying to explain differences in individual musical ability.

choices.text: fewer differences than similarities exist between the neurological processing of music and human language

choices.text: brain size increased rapidly over the course of human evolution
choices.explanation: Both authors would agree with this (third paragraph and sixth paragraph).

Passage B, paragraph 3 argues that premusical mother-infant interactions would have conferred considerable evolutionary advantage. Those positions support disagreement about great adaptive value; A need not deny every possible adaptive benefit.

choices.text: mother-infant bonding involves temporally patterned vocal interactions

choices.text: Why does it vary so greatly among different individuals?
choices.explanation: The author of passage A would have an answer (third paragraph), but the author of passage B does not take a position.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following principles underlies the arguments in both passages?

choices.explanation: Neither passage discusses nonhuman animals.

choices.text: All human capacities can be explained in terms of the evolutionary advantages they offer.
choices.explanation: Both passages assume that some human capacities can be explained in terms of the evolutionary advantages they confer (third and sixth paragraph), but neither assumes this to be true for all human capacities.

choices.explanation: Passage B expresses a stronger commitment to its hypothesis than does passage A (paragraph 3 and 6).
